01 — THE BASICS

A TFSA is a container,
not one kind of account.

“Tax-Free Savings Account” sounds like it only holds cash. Think of it more like a tax wrapper: the money can sit in different eligible savings or investment products, depending on the TFSA you open.

CRA: What is a TFSA? ↗
▤A / EASY ACCESS

Cash & GICs

A deposit TFSA can work like a savings account or GIC. A simple place to start learning about the account wrapper.

$
⌁B / INVESTMENTS

Eligible investments

A self-directed TFSA can hold eligible investments such as stocks, bonds, mutual funds and ETFs. Values can rise or fall.

✳

Tax-free doesn’t mean risk-free. The account changes the tax treatment; it doesn’t guarantee a return or protect an investment from losing value.

02 — YOUR CONTRIBUTION ROOM

Room is a limit
that adds up.

Your contribution room is the most you can put into all your TFSAs without an over-contribution. It belongs to you—not to each account separately.

i

Keep your own tally. CRA records can lag: institutions report transactions after the year ends, so the CRA account may not show this year’s activity yet.

Your room starts accumulating in the year you turn 18 while you are a Canadian tax resident. Unused room carries forward.

03 — AVOID THE OOPS

Two little rules
save a lot of stress.

Easy to miss when you’re new. Worth remembering.

01

Check the room before you add money.

Going over your available room can trigger a tax of 1% per month on the excess amount while it stays in the account. Check your own records and count contributions to every TFSA.

CRA: If you over-contribute ↗
!
02

Don’t automatically put a withdrawal back.

A withdrawal usually restores room on January 1 of the next calendar year. Re-contribute sooner only if you have other available room.

CRA: Withdrawals & room ↗

04 — YOUR FIRST FEW STEPS

Start small.
Stay curious.

You don’t need a perfect strategy to understand the account. Take it one step at a time.

✳ Your TFSA is yours to use for goals that matter to you.
  1. 01
    Check that you’re eligible.

    Generally, you need to be a Canadian tax resident, have a valid SIN and be at least 18. In some places, you may need to wait until 19 to enter the account contract; room from age 18 carries forward.

  2. 02
    Find your actual contribution room.

    Use your own records and CRA’s calculator. Remember every TFSA you have, not just the one you’re opening.

  3. 03
    Compare account options.

    Ask about fees, access to your money, interest or investment choices, and any minimum balance.

  4. 04
    Choose what goes inside.

    Cash, a GIC, or eligible investments have different features and risks. Make sure you understand the product before you buy it.

  5. 05
    Keep a simple contribution log.

    Record deposits and withdrawals as they happen. Re-check your room before making another contribution.

A FEW COMMON QUESTIONS

Quick answers.

Do I need a job to open or contribute?

No earned income is required. You do need to meet the CRA’s other eligibility conditions and stay within your available room.

Is $7,000 my personal limit for 2026?

Not necessarily. $7,000 is the annual limit added for 2026. You may also have unused room from earlier years, or you may have already used some of your room. Your personal available amount is based on your full history.

Does investment growth use more room?

No. The room tracks contributions—not investment growth. But the value of investments can go down, and special tax rules can apply in unusual situations.

Can I have more than one TFSA?

Yes, but there is one combined contribution limit. Add together contributions to all your TFSAs before deciding what you can contribute.

What if I’m not a Canadian tax resident?

Residency affects TFSA contributions and room. Check the CRA’s guidance for non-residents before contributing; don’t assume your usual room rules apply.
